problem: Learned navigation policies are hard to retarget to new goals at deployment. Prior hybrids of learning and topological-graph planning (SPTM, SoRB, LSTN, PRM-RL) assume one of three things: a simulator replica of the environment, online data collection, or simplified or discrete action spaces. They break down when trained only on offline, real-world image data that varies strongly in appearance.
motivation: Real robots in unstructured outdoor terrain cannot rely on geometry alone. Tall grass looks like an obstacle but is traversable, and a leaf-filled hole looks flat but is not. Collecting data online or in simulation is costly and unsafe. Humans navigate previously seen places from first-person views using landmark-based 'mental maps', and a goal photo is a natural way to specify a destination without GPS or maps.
key_idea: Learn a dynamical-distance (traversability) function and a relative-pose predictor purely from offline robot trajectories, then plan with Dijkstra over a pruned, non-metric topological graph of past images. Negative mining across trajectories makes the distance function robust to the distribution shift that graph building introduces.
insight: The general recipe is the same as SPTM/SoRB; the offline real-world success comes from three small changes. (1) Negative mining: pairs from different trajectories labelled d_max. (2) Graph pruning: easily traversable edges are dropped. (3) A mid-level waypoint action space: relative pose plus a PD controller instead of direct actions. In the ablation (Table II) at 50 m, full ViNG ('Waypoint') reaches 0.81, versus 0.52 without pruning, 0.43 with positives only, and 0.40 / 0.45 with direct continuous / discrete actions. Supervised versus TD distance learning makes little difference (0.81 vs 0.87 at 50 m). For new environments, combining source and target experience is essential: Finetune scores 0.79–0.96, Source-only 0–0.27, Target-only 0.32–0.44.
method: Traversability / dynamical distance function T(o_i,o_j): MobileNet encoder on a stack of two consecutive 160x120 RGB frames, then 3 FC layers classifying the temporal distance into 50 bins (d_max=50) with cross-entropy. Trained either supervised on the time-step gap within a trajectory, or with TD learning.

Negative mining (key idea 1): adds dataset D_- of observation pairs from different trajectories, labelled d_max. This counters the distribution shift from comparing observations across trajectories and times of day during graph construction.
Topological graph with pruning (key idea 2): nodes are previously observed images and edges are weighted by T. Edges with T < δ_sparsify are pruned to avoid quadratic growth and redundancy.

Planning: the current and goal images are localized by linking them to their most-traversable neighbors. Weighted Dijkstra computes the shortest path, and the first waypoint image goes to the controller.

Controller: a relative-pose predictor P (shared MobileNet encoder, FC head regressing Δx, Δy) is trained with L2 loss on odometry-derived labels for nearby pairs. A PD controller then uses odometry to steer toward the predicted waypoint pose with continuous linear/angular velocity.

Adaptation (ViNG-Finetune): in a new environment a human first teleoperates to collect initial data. The robot then autonomously practices reaching randomly sampled previously seen images, and T and P are finetuned on old plus new experience after each episode.

setting.backbone: MobileNet encoder + fully connected heads (traversability classifier and relative-pose regressor, shared encoder), trained on offline robot data
setting.training_data: 40 hours of offline, self-supervised real-world Jackal trajectories from BADGR (Kahn et al. 2020), collected more than 10 months before the experiments. Positive pairs come from within trajectories and negative pairs from across trajectories. For generalization, each new environment adds human-teleoperated exploration data plus autonomously self-collected practice data (up to 60 min).
setting.observation: monocular forward-facing 170° FOV RGB camera (two stacked consecutive 160x120 frames) + goal image; wheel odometry used by the low-level PD controller
setting.action_space: continuous linear and angular velocity (PD controller toward predicted relative-pose waypoint)
setting.simulator: real world (main experiments); Unity-based photorealistic outdoor simulator for comparison with online RL
setting.privileged: Pre-collected trajectories/images of the environment are required to build the topological graph (prior exploration); wheel odometry at test time. GPS and LiDAR are used only as safety mechanisms during data collection.

numbers_note: The main real-world comparison against SPTM, off-SoRB, State Estimator and Random (Fig. 3) and the simulated comparison against PPO and online SoRB (Fig. 7) are given only as figures. The only number stated in the text is ViNG's 86% on the hardest tasks. The Table II ablation does not state its exact evaluation setup; its caption refers to real-world performance, and its 50 m value (0.81) differs from the 86% in the text. All benchmarks are custom real-world outdoor evaluations, not standard benchmarks. Success metrics are printed as fractions and were converted to 0-100.
results: In the real-world urban/off-road environment, trained only on 40 h of 10-month-old offline data, ViNG reaches goals more than 40 m away where SPTM and offline SoRB fail. The text reports 86% success on the hardest tasks (results otherwise shown in Fig. 3). In four unseen environments, ViNG-Finetune with 60 min of new data reaches 0.79–0.96 success, beating SPTM-Finetune (0.56–0.74). In simulation it matches online SoRB, which needs 200 h of online data versus ViNG's 40 h offline, and it beats PPO.
limitations: Requires a static, pre-collected set of observations from the target environment to build the graph (prior exploration); non-stationary appearance such as lighting changes and dynamic objects is not handled.

Small-scale, custom real-world evaluation (6 start-goal pairs × 3 trials) with a non-standard success metric (fraction of the expert trajectory completed); the main comparisons are reported only in figures.
New environments need finetuning with human teleoperation plus autonomous practice; zero-shot transfer (ViNG-Source) performs poorly (0–0.27).
